newsitem.title: CHINA: China winds up HK committee with peals of praise.
newsitem.headline: China winds up HK committee with peals of praise.

text.p: China on Friday disbanded the committee it set up to pave the way for the July 1 return of Hong Kong to Beijing rule, saying the hand-picked group had made a great success of preparing the region's post-colonial future.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin and other leaders joined in praise for the 150-strong Preparatory Committee of mainland communist officials and Hong Kong notables after a last session in Beijing's cavernous Great Hall of the People.
"The Preparatory Commission has completed its solemn duty," Jiang told members at a photocall before a celebratory banquet for the committee, which was set up on January 26, 1996.

Premier Li Peng, parliamentary head Qiao Shi and foreign minister Qian Qichen joined in congratulations for the committee and for Beijing's wisdom in charting the way to the end of British rule in Hong Kong.

"The ability of the Preparatory Committee to achieve complete success, is the result of the correct leadership and policies of the central party leadership with Comrade Jiang Zemin at the core," Qian said in a speech.

China's National People's Congress, or parliament, last week approved the scrapping of the Preparatory Committee, which had played a key role in creating the first Chinese government of Hong Kong since the region was seized by Britain 156 years ago.
Tung Chee-hwa, chosen as Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader by a 400-member caucus selected by the committee, joined in the thanks and self-praise that dominated the group's final session.

Tung joined Jiang in expressing confidence that Hong Kong's reversion to Chinese rule and its future prosperity would be an important step toward achieving Beijing's dream of reunification with its Nationalist-ruled island rival Taiwan.
The Hong Kong leader was on his first visit to Beijing since he took office but had no events planned with Chinese officials other than the final session and banquet, Hong Kong officials said.

Tung, who played a largely secondary role in the Preparatory Committee's last session, left behind in Hong Kong a bitter dispute over his handling of the media, a crackdown on young Chinese migrants, and legal challenges to his administration.
Less than two weeks after its return to Chinese rule, Hong Kong is embroiled in a public row with local media who accuse Tung of giving preferential treatment to mainland journalists.

An illegal influx of mainland Chinese children trying to join parents already in Hong Kong has prompted Tung to ram through a law allowing their deportation, but the new law has been slammed by lawyers, welfare pressure groups and human rights monitors.

No mention of such issues disturbed the final session of the Preparatory Committee, which had itself drawn fire in Hong Kong and abroad for deciding to dismiss the territory's elected lawmakers and replace them with a hand-picked Provisional Legislature.
The 60-member provisional legislative body, which is made up of pro-China and business figures, will this month face a court hearing challenging its legitimacy.

By scrapping the Preparatory Committee and other groups intended to help manage the Hong Kong handover, Beijing says it is making a reality of its pledge to grant the region a high degree of autonomy.

But China will continue to keep an eye on the booming capitalist city on its southern coast. Beijing said last week it had created a committee to monitor the Basic Law, the region's post-handover mini-constitution.
